planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring after the last frost in constantly moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in deep to partial shade; blue deinanthe emerges late and its soft new growth can be damaged by a late freeze, so wait until frost danger has fully passed.

Deinanthe caerulea is a rare Chinese woodland perennial in the hydrangea family, forming a slowly spreading clump of broad, quilted, dark green leaves topped in mid to late summer by nodding, waxy, violet-blue flowers held just above the foliage. It is a connoisseur's shade plant for consistently moist, cool woodland gardens, resenting both summer drought and waterlogged winter soil, and performs best where summers stay relatively mild. Mulch heavily to conserve soil moisture and protect the shallow rhizomes over winter; established clumps are slow to increase and are best left undisturbed for several years between divisions.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall or early spring in deep, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; false anemone is native to cool, moist mountain forests in Japan and struggles where summers are hot and humid, so give it the coolest, most sheltered shade position available.

Anemonopsis macrophylla forms an elegant clump of deeply divided, anemone-like leaves and sends up branched stems of nodding, waxy, lilac to mauve, cup-shaped flowers with contrasting darker purple stamens in mid to late summer. It is one of the most coveted specialty woodland perennials among shade-garden collectors for its refined texture and unusual bloom color, though it is notoriously slow to establish and intolerant of drought, root disturbance, or heavy clay. Site it in a permanently cool, humus-rich pocket alongside hostas and ferns, keep the root zone mulched year-round, and avoid dividing established clumps except to propagate, since plants may sulk for a season or two afterward.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; leopard Solomon's seal spreads by creeping rhizomes to form an evergreen groundcover and, unlike deciduous Polygonatum, keeps its foliage through winter in zones 7 and warmer.

Disporopsis fuscopicta is a low, arching Chinese relative of Solomon's seal grown for its glossy, dark green, lance-shaped leaves speckled and mottled with maroon-purple blotches, with small, dangling, greenish-cream bells appearing beneath the foliage in spring followed by dark berries. It is a choice, slow-spreading evergreen groundcover for shaded borders and woodland gardens in the warmer half of the country, holding its patterned foliage year-round where winters are mild. Water regularly during dry spells, mulch to retain soil moisture, and divide congested clumps in early spring to spread the planting or share with other gardeners.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial shade; king Solomon's seal is one of the tallest and most vigorous Solomon's seal species and benefits from staking or the support of nearby shrubs once the arching stems reach full height.

Polygonatum kingianum is a dramatic Chinese woodland species with thick, knobby rhizomes (dried and used in traditional Chinese medicine as Huang Jing) and tall, gracefully arching stems lined with whorled leaves, hung in late spring with clusters of tubular orange-red to pink flowers that are showier than most Solomon's seals. It thrives in the dappled shade of a woodland border or shrub understory and tolerates summer heat and humidity better than many Asian Polygonatum species, making it a good choice for warm-temperate gardens. Established clumps expand steadily by rhizome and can be divided every three to four years in fall to control spread or increase the planting.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline woodland soil in partial to full shade; whorled Solomon's seal has an upright, unbranched habit rather than the arching form of most Polygonatum and reads as a strong vertical accent among lower shade groundcovers.

Polygonatum verticillatum is a Eurasian woodland species with narrow leaves arranged in tiers of whorls up a stiffly upright stem, producing small, pendant, greenish-white to pale pink tubular flowers in the leaf axils in late spring followed by red berries in fall. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form an open colony and is well suited to woodland gardens, shaded rock gardens, and the base of deciduous shrubs where its distinctive whorled, tiered foliage sets it apart from other Solomon's seals. Give it consistent moisture during the growing season and a leaf-litter mulch to mimic its native forest floor habitat.
